job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Beth Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Oh, mornings start with the hens. I live with Mum and Dad on their small dairy farm outside Alderfield, in the room I had as a kid, and I do the egg round before breakfast. I studied business and marketing with a good result, and did six weeks in the office of the Alderfield Farmers' Co-op, doing invoices and member letters. Now I apply for jobs after lunch, sing in the church choir on Wednesdays, and see my boyfriend Joel, a mechanic, on weekends. Dad can't help with my loan, because the milk price is low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's a relief, and I'd keep things steady. At church I'd say that we should keep looking after each other, because the real troubles are rent and milk prices, not robots. I'd tell Joel that his garage is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, nothing changing is not the same as nothing hurting. The Co-op has no spare post, the credit union in town has one opening that's gone to someone's cousin, and my loan is thick. I'm twenty-three and still living in my childhood bedroom, which I love and also find hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, especially to the credit union, the Co-op, the vet's office and the council in the market town. I'd ask Mr Hollis at the Co-op for a coffee and tell him I'm ready for any post, even part-time. I'd also take the Saturday shifts at the farm shop, and help Dad with the milk records so that he can see I'm useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit low, in a quiet way. I'm not panicked, but there's a grey cloud on Sunday evenings when everyone talks about work on Monday. Joel's patient, but I know he'd like us to move forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does moving forward mean for you and Joel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wedding, in about two years, and a small flat in town. We've talked about it honestly. I want to have a proper job and the loan under control before we plan anything, and Joel agrees. So every month without a job is a month the wedding slides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Mr Hollis at the Co-op to know about you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm steady and I learn. I did the invoices and the member letters and never missed a deadline in six weeks. I'm also not afraid to learn new software, as long as someone shows me once or twice. I'd just like him to remember me when a post comes up.

say: I'd say we should **look after** each other, because rent and milk prices are the real troubles.
I'd tell Joel his **garage** is safe.
think: Nothing changing is not the same as **nothing hurting**.
The Co-op has no spare post and my **loan** is thick.
do: Apply to the **credit union**, the Co-op, the vet's office and the council.
Ask Mr Hollis at the Co-op for a **coffee**.
Take **Saturday shifts** at the farm shop.
feel: A **quiet low**, with a grey cloud on Sunday evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we should walk into it with our eyes open. At church I'd ask for the young ones to be helped, because the entry jobs will be the first to go. I'd say people shouldn't be afraid to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it worries me. The Co-op already uses software to send member letters and track invoices, which was my whole six weeks. If they need fewer people for that, there's no post for me. But I use AI tools now and then, for letters and summaries, and they're a help, so I know I can learn more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the tools seriously: I'd do a short course on business software and AI through the library, and practise on the farm's records. I'd apply to jobs that involve talking to customers or members, because people like a person at the counter. And I'd ask the credit union if there's any apprenticeship or training scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. I'm a bit scared, but I'm also a bit pleased with myself that I can learn it. I'd lie awake thinking about the Co-op letters and then get up and practise on a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why jobs where you talk to people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in a small town, trust matters. If your neighbour hands over her savings at the credit union, she wants someone she knows to say it's fine. Software can't sit with Mrs Lindqvist and listen to her worry. I think those jobs last longer, though they aren't easy to find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dad about the dairy farm in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep the milk records on the app, because it saves time, and let me help with it. I wouldn't tell him to change the farm. But he's slow to try new things, and I'd gently show him one new thing at a time, like the feed calculator.

I'd say the **young ones** need help, because entry jobs go first.

I already use AI for letters, so I know I can **learn more**.

Apply for jobs that involve **talking to members** and customers.
Ask the credit union about a **training scheme**.
feel: **Mixed**: scared, but a bit proud that she can learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and families need help now. At church I'd say we pray, but also make real plans for the people who lose work. I'd tell Dad not to take on new debt on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm frightened. Two years means I'm twenty-five, my degree is for work machines do, and the loan is still there. Joel's garage is safe for longer, but the thinking jobs go first, and mine are thinking jobs. The wedding would slip and slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get any paid work now, farm shop, cleaning, anything, and save every pound. I'd talk to Mum and Dad about staying on the farm as long as needed and doing more of the dairy work. I'd also ask the church and my aunt about whether the credit union has any plan for people in my position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaky. I keep seeing the day I'd tell Mum that all the study didn't work out. I'd feel guilty for her sacrifice, because she cleaned houses to help me through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you see yourself on the dairy farm long term?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not as a plan, but I'd help. I grew up there, I can do milk records, books, and I'm not scared of cows. If the thinking jobs go and robots take three years more, then the farm and the shop might be the last places that need a person. It would be a different life from the one I studied for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen with Joel and the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd wait, I think. Joel would still be earning, so maybe we'd marry smaller. But I wouldn't want to start a household in debt without a job. We'd cut the wedding to a church service and a tea in the hall. I'd rather have a simple day than a heavy start.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and families need help now.
I'd tell Dad not to take on new **debt** on the farm.
think: My degree is for work machines do, and the **loan** is still there.
Thinking jobs go first, and **mine** are thinking jobs.

Do more of the **dairy work** at home.

feel: **Shaky**, and guilty about her mother's sacrifice.
S2.quote: I'd rather have a simple day than a heavy start.
fieldNote: Her fear is about **letting down** her mother, who cleaned houses for her study.

steps.text: Take any paid work, such as the farm shop or cleaning, and save
Do more of the milk records and dairy work at home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to plan, and we should plan as families and as a church. I'd tell Dad to think about whether the farm can pay for itself. I'd say to young people, learn something practical and something to do with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years could be enough. If I get a post this year, I'd have two or three years, enough to pay a good part of the loan and marry. I'd just need to stay useful, and I think I'm steady enough to do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a post soon, in a credit union or the Co-op, and learn the whole operation. I'd take a course on the new tools so I can show I'm ready. I'd save three hundred a month and look at a flat with Joel in about three years, and keep some of the Sundays free for choir and family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, and a little nervous. It feels like when you plant seed and you can't see the shoots yet. I'd rather be planting than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you make yourself useful in a credit union as things change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By being the person members trust, and also the one who can explain what the software has done. I'd learn the lending rules and the community, because people come in for advice. A machine can approve a loan, but I'd want to be the one who says why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you picture the next year differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two-year picture I'd grab money and hunker down. In this one I'd invest in myself: courses, a first post, a savings habit and a wedding plan. There's room to plan, and I'd use it.

say: I'd say five years is **time to plan**, as families and as a church.
I'd tell young people to learn something **practical** and something about money.
think: Five years could be enough: a post this year, then **two or three years** to pay and marry.

Take a course on the **new tools**.
Save **three hundred** a month toward a flat with Joel.
feel: **Hopeful** and a little nervous, like planting seed and waiting for shoots.
S3.quote: A machine can approve a loan, but I'd want to be the one who says why.
fieldNote: Her goal is to be the **trusted human** next to the software.

steps.text: Take a post at the credit union or the Co-op and learn lending rules
Do a course on the new tools
Save three hundred a month toward a flat with Joel
Plan the wedding for three years' time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, and we should use it to teach the young and look after the old. At church I'd say keep faith, keep working, and don't panic. I'd tell Dad that the farm can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years feels fine. I could build a career, marry Joel, maybe have children and pay off my loan. The world would change but I'd have time to change with it, one small step at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a post, keep learning, and aim for a proper career at the credit union or something like it. I'd take a new course every second year. And I'd marry Joel in two or three years, buy a small house in town and keep the farm connection, helping Dad's accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's the first one where I think we'd be okay. I'd still say my prayers every night, but with less worry in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would family life look like in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small house near the market, two kids maybe, Sunday lunch at the farm. Joel would keep his garage going, and I'd have work I trust. I'd like my children to learn that people matter more than machines, even good ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from now if you knew you had ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop being so hard on myself. I've been counting months without a post as failures, when really they're part of a long road. I'd take the first decent job and not wait for the perfect one.

say: I'd say ten years is a **blessing** to teach the young and look after the old.
I'd tell Dad the **farm** can plan.
think: Ten years feels **fine**: career, marriage, maybe children, and the loan paid.
The world changes but I'd change with it, one **small step** at a time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because two years doesn't give me time for a job, my loan or my wedding. What would help is a loan freeze while I'm job hunting, a training scheme at the credit union or Co-op, and honest warning from leaders so families can plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people in small towns aren't behind, we're just far from the jobs. If somebody gives us a chance and a bit of patience, we learn.

headlineQuote: People in small towns aren't behind, we're just far from the jobs. If somebody gives us a chance and a bit of patience, we learn.
portrait: Beth, 23, has a **good business degree**, six weeks at a farmers' co-op, and lives on her parents' dairy farm.
She is warm and church-going, and hopes to marry her boyfriend Joel, a mechanic.
She uses AI tools **now and then** and learns best when someone shows her once or twice.
Her mood is anxious or alarmed because the loan is heavy, local jobs are few and the wedding waits.
She wants to be the **trusted human** beside the software, and in ten years feels near calm.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most: no time for a job, the loan or the wedding.
whatWouldHelp: A **loan freeze** while job hunting, a training scheme at the credit union or Co-op, and honest warning.
